overview.text: The Federalist Papers, also called The Federalist, are 85 essays written by Alexander Hamilton, James Madison, and John Jay and published anonymously under the shared name Publius. Printed in New York newspapers in 1787–1788, they urged New Yorkers to ratify the proposed Constitution and answered objections raised during the debate. The essays explained how parts of the new government were intended to work, including how a large republic might manage competing interests and how separated branches could check one another. Their significance extends beyond the ratification campaign: historians and readers use them as an important source for understanding arguments about the Constitution, though they are essays advocating a position, not a neutral record of everyone’s views.

key_facts.text: The essays appeared in New York newspapers and were later collected in a two-volume edition.
Publius was a shared pen name for Hamilton, Madison, and Jay; the essays were published anonymously.
The essays promoted ratification amid opposition that included concerns about central power and the absence of a bill of rights.
Federalist No. 10 discusses factions and the possibility of governing a large republic.
The Library of Congress describes the essays as an important source for interpreting the Constitution’s intentions.
